one_liner: Research and write policy memos and briefings on financial stability and financial regulation for Treasury's Financial Stability Oversight Council staff in DC.
fit_summary: Daniel's policy knowledge, writing for government clients, and relationship skills match the briefing and stakeholder-contact duties, but every grade requires specialized experience in financial markets, financial institutions, or U.S. financial regulatory policy. Emergency-management consulting at IEM is unlikely to count unless Daniel did real work on disaster finance, grant funding, or financial regulation. The GS-11 level is the only realistic target, and only with genuine financial-sector content.
eligibility: Open to the public (U.S. citizens/nationals), so Daniel needs no federal status; a clearance is not required, but a background investigation and confidential financial disclosure are.
GS-11 requires one year of GS-9-level experience researching and analyzing financial markets or financial institutions AND writing policy analysis on them.
GS-12 and GS-13 require one year of next-lower-grade experience with U.S. financial regulatory policy and engagement with financial regulatory agencies.
Education can substitute only with a Ph.D., 3 years of related doctoral-level graduate study, or a related LL.M.; a combination of experience and education is assessed in the questionnaire.
Must pass an online competency assessment and reach the cut-off score of 89 to be referred.
strategy: Apply at GS-11 only, unless Daniel can document a full year of work with financial regulators. Answer the questionnaire honestly, because overstating experience can remove you from consideration.

Inventory your IEM work for any financial content, such as disaster recovery funding, FEMA/HUD grant financial analysis, insurance, or economic impact. Frame only true examples as research on financial institutions or markets.
Emphasize policy writing for management: briefing papers, memos, and reports you drafted for government clients, using the posting's exact phrases.
Fit everything on two pages. For each job, list month/day/year dates and hours per week, plus 3-5 bullets tied to the specialized experience.
Prepare for the online competency assessment, which covers reading comprehension, reasoning, and attention to detail. The window is short, so submit before November 4, 2026 (opens October 26).
Treat this as a stretch. Also target policy-analyst roles closer to your background, such as FEMA, DHS, Virginia VDEM, NoVA local emergency management, or legislative offices.
resume_bullets: Researched and analyzed [topic, e.g., disaster recovery funding flows / insurance market impacts] for [client agency], producing [number] briefing papers and memoranda that informed [type of policy decision].
Monitored [legislative/regulatory] developments affecting [program area] and summarized findings in [charts, short summaries, reports] for [audience, e.g., client leadership].
Maintained working contacts with [Federal/State agencies] to coordinate [policy or program implementation], contributing to a [size]-person team-based project on [subject].
interview_questions: Describe a time you turned complex research into a short memo for a senior decision-maker. What did you leave out and why?
What do you see as current risks to U.S. financial stability, and what is FSOC's role in addressing them?
How would you assess the effect of a proposed financial regulation on the financial system?
Tell us about coordinating with outside agencies or stakeholders who had competing priorities.
watch_outs: Specialized experience is heavily finance-specific, so emergency-management consulting alone will likely rate not qualified.
The application window is short: it opens October 26 and closes November 4, 2026.
The cut-off score of 89, the online assessment, and veterans' preference ordering make referral competitive for non-preference applicants.
The duty station is Washington, DC, with telework but not remote work, so expect a commute from Manassas for in-office days.
